sections.h2: What the Minnesota homestead exemption covers
sections.html:
Minnesota uses the word homestead for two separate protections. One shields a home from most creditors under Chapter 510. The other is a property tax classification that the county assessor grants under Minn. Stat. 273.124, and it lowers the taxable value of the house. A seller usually meets both at the same closing table.

Section 510.01 protects the house a debtor owns and occupies as a dwelling, plus the land under it within stated limits, from seizure or sale for debts not charged against it in writing. The carve-outs in that same section are debts for work or materials that went into building, repairing or improving the homestead, and wages owed to laborers or servants.

Under Minn. Stat. 510.02, a homestead may include up to 160 acres, and the exemption may not exceed $540,000 per homestead. If the homestead is used mainly for agriculture, the cap rises to $1,350,000. These dollar figures are adjusted periodically and the commissioner of commerce publishes the changes, so confirm the current number before relying on an older one.

The exemption has edges. Under Minn. Stat. 510.05, it is not reduced by, and does not reach, the following:

  • a mortgage lawfully placed on the home;
  • a valid lien for taxes or assessments;
  • claims for state hospital care or medical assistance filed under sections 246.53 or 256B.15;
  • charges that arise under the laws on laborers' or material suppliers' liens.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for homestead classification and how to apply
sections.html:
Residential real estate occupied and used as a homestead by its owner, who must be a Minnesota resident, is a residential homestead under Minn. Stat. 273.124, subdivision 1. An owner who meets that test must file a homestead application with the county assessor to get the classification the first time. Each owner who lives in the home signs it, and so does each occupying owner's spouse.

The assessor also needs the Social Security number or individual taxpayer identification number of each occupying owner, plus the name and number of that owner's spouse. If the spouse's details are left off the form, the owners are treated as having chosen only partial homestead treatment, and the rest of the house is classified as nonhomestead residential.

A relative of the owner can also make the house a homestead. The statute lists a parent, stepparent, child, stepchild, grandparent, grandchild, brother, sister, uncle, aunt, nephew or niece, by blood or marriage. The tax treatment then matches what the owner would receive if the owner lived there, and neither the owner nor the relative may claim a chapter 290A refund on that property.

sections.h2: The December 31 deadline for a newly bought home
sections.html:
A house that was not a homestead on the assessment date but was used as one on December 31 is class 1 or 2a for that year, and the owner must notify the county assessor in writing by December 31 of the year of occupancy. That rule is in subdivision 9 of Minn. Stat. 273.124. The assessor cannot deny full treatment to a property that was partly homesteaded on January 2 but fully occupied as a homestead on December 31.

With no homestead application on file by December 31, the assessor classifies the property as nonhomestead for taxes payable the following year. The assessor must publish a notice by December 1 each year reminding owners of the filing requirement.

  • File the homestead application with the county assessor, not the city clerk.
  • Have every occupying owner and spouse sign.
  • Send the written notice before December 31 if you moved in after the January 2 assessment date.

sections.h2: What homestead status saves on a tax bill
sections.html:
The saving comes through a market value exclusion in Minn. Stat. 273.13, subdivision 35. For a homestead valued at $95,000 or less, the exclusion is 40 percent of market value. Between $95,000 and $517,200, the exclusion is $38,000 minus nine percent of the value above $95,000. At $517,200 or more there is no exclusion. The taxable value is what is left after the exclusion, before the classification rate is applied.

Homestead classification lasts until the property is sold or transferred, or until the owners, their spouses or the qualifying relatives stop using it as a homestead. Minn. Stat. 273.124 requires the owner to tell the assessor within 30 days of a sale, a transfer or a move-out. Missing that window carries a penalty and ends the homestead status.

The creditor protection follows the money for a limited time. Under Minn. Stat. 510.07, the owner may sell and convey the homestead without exposing the proceeds, for one year after the sale, to debts the homestead was exempt from. Court-ordered child support or maintenance in arrears is the exception. Insurance proceeds on an exempt homestead are exempt for one year as well.

An owner who moves out has a clock running. If the owner stops occupying the home for more than six consecutive months, the home is treated as abandoned unless the owner files a notice with the county recorder claiming it as the homestead. The exemption never continues more than five years after that filing unless the family actually lived there for part of the term.

At closing, whenever the price is above $3,000, the grantor, grantee or their agent files a certificate of value with the county auditor when the deed is presented for recording (Minn. Stat. 272.115).

sections.h2: Property tax refund and senior deferral
sections.html:
The homestead credit refund in Minn. Stat. 290A.04 pays when property taxes exceed a set percentage of household income. The percentage starts at 1.0 percent of income for the lowest brackets and climbs to 2.5 percent in the highest. The maximum refund is $3,310 for household incomes up to $50,099 and steps down through the brackets, to $650 for incomes from $130,350 to $135,409. Households at $135,410 or more receive nothing.

Payment timing is set in Minn. Stat. 290A.07. Most claimants are paid after September 15 and before September 30. Owners of manufactured homes are paid after August 1 and before August 15, or 60 days after the application arrives, whichever is later.

Older owners have a separate option. The senior citizens' deferral in Minn. Stat. 290B.03 requires these conditions:

  • the owner is 65 or older, and in a married couple one spouse is at least 65 and the other at least 62;
  • household income for the year before the first application is $96,000 or less;
  • the home has been the owner's homestead for at least five years;
  • there are no state or federal tax liens or judgment liens on it;
  • debts secured by the property do not exceed 75 percent of the assessor's estimated market value.

sections.h2: What happens to a homestead after the owner dies?
sections.html:
If there is a surviving spouse, Minn. Stat. 524.2-402 sends the homestead to the spouse when the decedent left no descendants. When descendants survive, the spouse holds it for life and the remainder goes to the descendants in equal shares by representation. With no spouse and no will covering it, the homestead descends like other real estate.

A homestead that passes to the spouse, the descendants or a trust for them alone is exempt from debts that were not valid charges on it at death, except the state hospital and medical assistance claims mentioned above. A homestead that passes to anyone else answers for administration expenses, funeral costs, last illness expenses, taxes and debts. A personal representative selling a homestead in which a spouse takes an interest needs the spouse's written consent, as Minn. Stat. 524.3-715 spells out in clause 23.

An owner who missed the filing and finds the error later can ask the county board for relief. Minn. Stat. 375.192 lets the board reduce or abate value or taxes on written application, but for the two prior years only in cases of clerical error or hardship, and the assessor and county auditor must approve the application first.

faqs.q: How much is the Minnesota homestead exemption worth against creditors?
faqs.a: It is capped at $540,000 per homestead, or $1,350,000 if the property is used mainly for agriculture, on up to 160 acres. The commissioner of commerce publishes adjustments to those figures, so check the current amount. The cap never reaches mortgages, valid tax or assessment liens, or mechanics' lien charges.

faqs.q: Do I have to reapply for Minnesota homestead classification every year?
faqs.a: No. Once granted, the classification stays until the property is sold or transferred or the owners stop living there. The assessor can still ask at any time for a new application to confirm that the property qualifies, and a name change or transfer may trigger a fresh request.

faqs.q: How soon must I tell the assessor after I sell or move out of a Minnesota home?
faqs.a: Within 30 days. Missing that deadline brings a penalty, and the property loses its homestead status. Send the notice to the county assessor and keep proof of the date you sent it.

faqs.q: Can a relative living in my Minnesota house get homestead treatment?
faqs.a: Yes, to the extent the treatment would apply if the owner lived there. The owner must file a homestead application with the relative's details, and if a different relative moves in, the owner must notify the assessor within 30 days. Neither person can claim a property tax refund for that home.

faqs.q: Are my Minnesota sale proceeds safe from creditors after closing?
faqs.a: For one year after the sale, the proceeds are protected from debts the homestead was exempt from. Court-ordered child support or maintenance arrears are not protected. After that year, ordinary creditors can reach the money unless another exemption applies.
